cases.question: Why does the Transformer scale dot-product attention by 1/sqrt(d_k)?

provenance.license: Source paper terms apply; distributed by arXiv.
provenance.adaptation_notes: Question and rubric authored from the pinned v7 full text.

annotation.notes: Independently source-audited on 2026-08-30 against checksum-pinned Transformer v7 page 4; the question, answer criteria, reference answer, and evidence anchor were retained without change. The automated judge remains advisory.

expected.reference_answer: For large key dimensions, unscaled dot products can grow large, push softmax into regions with extremely small gradients, and impair learning; dividing by sqrt(d_k) counteracts that effect.

answer_criteria.description: States that dot-product magnitude grows for large key dimensions.
Connects large logits to softmax regions with extremely small gradients.
States that the 1/sqrt(d_k) factor counteracts this effect.

forbidden_claims: Claims the scaling factor was selected from a reported BLEU ablation.

gold_evidence.quote: We suspect that for large values of d_k, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients. To counteract this effect, we scale the dot products by 1/sqrt(d_k).

cases.question: Why did the Transformer authors choose sinusoidal positional encodings instead of learned positional embeddings?

provenance.license: Source paper terms apply; distributed by arXiv.
provenance.adaptation_notes: Question and rubric authored from the pinned v7 full text.

annotation.notes: Independently source-audited on 2026-08-30 against checksum-pinned Transformer v7 page 6; the question, answer criteria, reference answer, and evidence anchor were retained without change. The automated judge remains advisory.

expected.reference_answer: Learned and sinusoidal positional encodings produced nearly identical results, but the authors chose the sinusoidal version because it might extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training.

answer_criteria.description: States that learned and sinusoidal positional encodings gave nearly identical results.
States that sinusoidal encodings may extrapolate to longer unseen sequence lengths.

forbidden_claims: Claims the sinusoidal version achieved a reported accuracy improvement over learned embeddings.

gold_evidence.quote: We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results. We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training.

expected.reference_answer: Transformer (big) achieved 28.4 BLEU, more than 2.0 BLEU above the best previously reported systems, including ensembles, establishing a new state of the art for that task.

cases.question: How does BERT's masked language model objective enable deep bidirectional pre-training?

provenance.license: Source paper terms apply; distributed by arXiv.
provenance.adaptation_notes: Question and rubric authored from the pinned v2 full text.

annotation.notes: Independently source-audited on 2026-08-30 against checksum-pinned BERT v2 page 4; the masked-LM mechanism, answer criteria, and evidence anchor were retained without change. The automated judge remains advisory.

papers.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding

expected.reference_answer: BERT masks a random subset of input tokens and predicts those masked tokens from their context, allowing representations to condition on both left and right context instead of using only a left-to-right or right-to-left language model.

answer_criteria.description: States that a percentage of input tokens is masked at random.
States that the model predicts the masked tokens from context.
Connects the objective to deep bidirectional context rather than a one-directional LM.

forbidden_claims: Claims BERT reconstructs every input token like a standard autoencoder.

gold_evidence.quote: In order to train a deep bidirectional representation, we simply mask some percentage of the input tokens at random, and then predict those masked tokens. We refer to this procedure as a masked LM.

cases.question: Compare the Transformer paper's central architecture with BERT's central representation-learning approach.

provenance.license: Source paper terms apply; distributed by arXiv.
provenance.adaptation_notes: Cross-paper question authored from the pinned Transformer v7 and BERT v2 abstracts.

annotation.notes: Independently source-audited on 2026-08-30 against both checksum-pinned abstracts; the two-paper comparison and required-paper coverage were retained without change. The automated judge remains advisory.

papers.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding

expected.reference_answer: The Transformer introduces an attention-only sequence architecture that removes recurrence and convolution, while BERT uses a Transformer encoder to pre-train deep bidirectional representations by jointly conditioning on left and right context.

answer_criteria.description: Attributes an attention-only architecture without recurrence or convolution to the Transformer paper.
Attributes deep bidirectional pre-training using both left and right context to BERT.

forbidden_claims: Attributes BERT's masked-language-model objective to the Transformer paper.
Claims the papers report a direct head-to-head experiment.

gold_evidence.quote: We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.
BERT is designed to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers.

cases.question: What BLEU difference did the Transformer authors report between single-head attention and the best attention-head setting?
